studies.title: Anxiety disorders and PTSD are linked to a higher risk of stroke, in a pooled analysis of 11 million people
studies.ns_score_reason: huge sample and a clean effect size, but observational cohorts only, so causation stays open.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Researchers pooled 23 longitudinal cohort studies covering 11,181,338 participants to test whether anxiety disorders, OCD, and PTSD predict a first-ever stroke. Clinically diagnosed anxiety disorders were associated with a 29% higher hazard of stroke, PTSD with 50%, and the association held specifically for ischemic (not hemorrhagic) stroke. Crucially, the effects persisted after adjustment for cardiovascular risk factors and for depression.
studies.why_it_matters: Fear- and stress-related disorders have mostly been treated as brain problems; this suggests they also travel with the vascular system, and that a psychiatric diagnosis may function as a vascular risk marker in its own right.
studies.pitch_angle: The surprise is that PTSD outperformed depression — the usual psychiatric suspect in cardiovascular risk — and the link survived adjustment for blood pressure, smoking and the rest. Open on someone in their forties with a long-standing anxiety diagnosis whose cardiology appointment never mentions it. Call Pankaj Sharma's group at Royal Holloway, and pair with a stroke epidemiologist who can say plainly what the residual confounding problem is. Frame it as a risk-marker question, not a "treat your anxiety to prevent stroke" claim.
studies.wider_angle: A longer feature on whether psychiatry and cardiology should share a risk chart at all — the slow merging of "mental" and "cardiometabolic" risk scoring, and what a combined clinic would actually look like. Fits a health-policy or medical-trade outlet.
studies.caveats: Observational cohorts only (cannot establish causation); substantial heterogeneity between studies; OCD evidence rested on a single study; diagnoses defined differently across cohorts.

studies.title: Stress hormones show up in how other people rate your working relationships — not in how you rate them yourself
studies.ns_score_reason: an unusually rich behavioral dataset and a genuinely uncomfortable finding; limited by the small number of professionals.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Across four waves, 46 community supervision officers provided diurnal cortisol samples while independent observers rated relationship quality in 2126 video-recorded sessions with 732 supervisees; officers also rated 432 of those relationships themselves. Within individuals, higher total daily cortisol output predicted lower observer-rated caring and fairness, and a flatter cortisol slope predicted lower observer-rated trust. No cortisol measure predicted the officers' own ratings of the same relationships.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests physiological stress degrades the skilled, effortful part of professional interaction — and does so invisibly to the person doing it, because self-reports were largely trait-like and stable.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the blind spot: on your most physiologically stressed days, other people can see you being less fair and less trustworthy, and you can't. Open on a probation officer running back-to-back appointments. Call Frances Chen at Georgia State, and get a second voice on why self-report measures of relationship quality barely move within a person. Careful framing: this is covariation, not proof that cortisol causes worse behavior.
studies.wider_angle: A workplace feature on "relational labor" in high-stakes public-service jobs — probation, social work, emergency medicine — and the case for measuring quality of interaction by observation rather than staff surveys. Fits a public-administration or long-form labor outlet.
studies.caveats: Small N of professionals (46) despite thousands of sessions; observational within-person design; single occupational setting, may not generalize.

studies.title: A close bond with parents fails to protect stressed teenagers' response to reward
studies.ns_score_reason: a clear failure of a well-loved buffering hypothesis, with EEG plus behavior; effects are modest and the sample is mostly White.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: In 165 adolescents aged 9-16, researchers interviewed participants about parent-child relationship quality and exposure to peer stress, then measured reward responsiveness three ways: self-report, a behavioral reward-learning task, and the reward positivity brain response to money, social and food rewards. Contrary to prediction, teenagers with higher-quality parent-child relationships showed a *blunted* brain response to monetary reward and reduced behavioral reward sensitivity when they also reported high peer stress.
studies.why_it_matters: The "good parenting buffers social stress" story is close to received wisdom; this suggests it is not uniform, and that different measures of the reward system give different answers.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is the reversal — warm parents were associated with a *flatter* reward response in stressed teens, the opposite of the buffering prediction. Open on the lab scene: a 13-year-old in an EEG cap winning small sums of money after a week of being frozen out at school. Call Anna Weinberg at McGill and press her on the honest interpretation, including the possibility that protective parenting reduces the need to chase rewards elsewhere. No parenting advice should be drawn from it.
studies.wider_angle: A methods-driven feature for a psychology-literate audience on why self-report, behavior and brain measures of the same construct routinely disagree — and what that means for the RDoC-style project of building psychiatry out of "units of analysis."
studies.caveats: Small-to-moderate N (165); cross-sectional; predominantly White sample, may not generalize; several interactions non-significant, so the positive finding needs replication.

studies.title: Treating PTSD reduces physical pain — even when no one treats the pain
studies.ns_score_reason: randomized parent trial and a year of follow-up, but a secondary analysis with no pain-only control arm.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: A secondary analysis of a PTSD effectiveness trial in 196 veterans randomized to Prolonged Exposure plus placebo, Prolonged Exposure plus sertraline, or sertraline with enhanced medication management. Over 52 weeks, pain severity and interference fell in all three arms — including among the 70 and 93 veterans with clinically significant baseline pain interference and severity. Prolonged Exposure plus placebo produced the largest drop in pain interference during treatment.
studies.why_it_matters: Chronic pain and PTSD co-occur constantly and are usually managed in separate clinics; this is the first head-to-head look at whether PTSD-focused treatment moves pain, and the psychotherapy arm did at least as well as the drug.
studies.pitch_angle: Sell the counterintuitive clinical shape: talking through the trauma memory did more for pain interference than the antidepressant, in people who came in for PTSD, not pain. Open on a veteran whose back pain was treated for years as an orthopedic problem. Call Sheila Rauch at Emory. Be explicit that the study cannot rule out natural improvement over 52 weeks.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on the "pain is produced by the brain under threat" model and the clinicians trying to treat chronic pain by targeting fear and prediction rather than tissue — for a health or medical-science outlet, with the opioid-sparing angle built in.
studies.caveats: Secondary analysis of a trial not designed for pain outcomes; no non-treatment control, so improvement over time cannot be attributed to treatment; veteran sample, may not generalize; several authors declare pharma and foundation relationships (listed in the paper).

studies.title: Post-traumatic stress symptoms predict who moves from suicidal thoughts to an attempt
studies.ns_score_reason: a prospective sample of people already having suicidal thoughts is rare and valuable; effects are modest and all measures self-reported.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: 923 Australian adults with current suicidal ideation (mean age 36, 65% women) were assessed for depression, generalized and social anxiety, obsessive-compulsive, and post-traumatic stress symptoms, then followed every six months for 18 months with 86% retention. 11.5% reported a suicide attempt. Baseline post-traumatic stress symptoms carried the strongest hazard (HR 1.26) and depressive symptoms a smaller one, while obsessive-compulsive symptoms showed a small *negative* association with attempts.
studies.why_it_matters: Most suicide research compares people with ideation to the general population; this tests the far more useful question of who, among those already thinking about suicide, goes on to act — and hints that some anxiety-spectrum symptoms may inhibit rather than enable action.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is the OCD result running the "wrong" way, which fits the "capability for suicide" idea: harm-avoidance may hold people back. Open with the ideation-to-attempt transition as the thing clinicians most want to predict and least can. Call Philip Batterham at the Australian National University. Handle with standard suicide-reporting care, including help-line signposting, and avoid implying any symptom set is reassuring.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on why suicide prediction models have barely improved in 50 years of research, and the shift from risk factors toward theories of capability and acute state — a good fit for a psychiatry-focused or long-form science outlet.
studies.caveats: All measures self-reported including attempts; modest effect sizes; associations attenuated by lifetime attempt history; Australian community sample, may not generalize.

studies.title: About half of postpartum depression cases don't lift within the first year
studies.ns_score_reason: fine-grained repeated measures across 12 months is genuinely uncommon; N is moderate and single-center.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: 191 mothers were followed from childbirth through 12 months with repeated symptom measures plus assessments of mother-infant attachment and perceived stress. Roughly half of postpartum depression cases recovered within six months and the rest did not. Among initially healthy mothers, 4.7% developed major depression within the year; among those with an early adjustment disorder, 25.6% did. Persistent cases were marked by low attachment, low social support, prior depression, childhood maltreatment and premenstrual syndrome.
studies.why_it_matters: Postpartum depression is widely framed as a six-week window; this reframes it as a dynamic 12-month process with distinct recovery, persistence and late-onset paths — and identifies early adjustment disorder as a strong warning signal.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the timing problem: screening concentrated in the first six weeks misses the quarter of mothers with early adjustment difficulties who become depressed months later. Open on a mother cleared at her six-week check who deteriorates at month seven. Call Natalya Chechko at RWTH Aachen. Note the hormonal-sensitivity signature — baby blues plus PMS — as an observational pattern, not a test.
studies.wider_angle: A reported piece on how maternal mental health screening is scheduled across different health systems, and whether the first-year monitoring this study implies is affordable anywhere. Fits a health-service or parenting-oriented publication.
studies.caveats: Moderate N (191), single-center German cohort, may not generalize; observational; risk correlates are retrospective self-report.

studies.title: Inflammation in the body changes what brain-clearance markers mean in depressed teenage girls
studies.ns_score_reason: large, well-controlled imaging cohort; but the headline result is a moderation effect in a subgroup and needs replication.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: In the sBEAD cohort, 461 adolescents with major depression and 253 healthy controls underwent multimodal MRI measures of the brain's glymphatic clearance system alongside blood markers of inflammation and oxidative stress. Depressed adolescents showed altered perivascular diffusion, higher free water and a higher systemic immune-inflammation index. Larger choroid plexus volume was associated with more severe depression only in patients with high inflammation — and only in girls.
studies.why_it_matters: It links the immune system to the brain's waste-clearance machinery in adolescent depression, an interaction not previously shown in this age group; for now it is a mechanistic lead rather than anything clinical.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is that a brain structure's size means one thing in an inflamed body and nothing in a non-inflamed one — a reminder that neuroimaging markers may be conditional rather than absolute. Open on the glymphatic system as the brain's overnight cleaning crew. Call Liping Cao's group at Guangzhou Medical University; get an independent glymphatic-imaging researcher to say how contested the diffusion index is.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a science or medical outlet on the fast-moving and much-disputed field of human glymphatic imaging — what these MRI proxies actually measure, and why sleep researchers and psychiatrists are both staking claims on them.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional (cannot establish causation); the key effect is a sex-specific moderation, vulnerable to multiple-comparison concerns; single-region Chinese cohort, may not generalize; MRI glymphatic proxies remain methodologically contested.

studies.title: Childhood trauma shows up in teenagers' sleep years later — and perceived stress is the route
studies.ns_score_reason: proper longitudinal design with a physiological moderator; sex-specific effect is fragile.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: 284 adolescents reported childhood trauma and sleep quality at baseline, gave a physiological measure of vagal regulation (respiratory sinus arrhythmia suppression during a stressful speech task), and were reassessed 1.5 years later for perceived stress and sleep. Childhood trauma predicted worse sleep 18 months on even after controlling for baseline sleep, and perceived stress mediated the link. Among boys — but not girls — the stress-to-sleep link was weaker in those whose vagal "brake" engaged more strongly during the task.
studies.why_it_matters: It puts a measurable physiological marker on the path from early adversity to poor sleep, and suggests the vulnerable step is not the trauma itself but how stressful daily life subsequently feels.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the lab detail: how hard a teenager's vagus nerve pulls back during a three-minute speech task tracks how badly perceived stress will wreck his sleep a year and a half later. Open on the speech task itself. Call Wei Lü at Shaanxi Normal University. Keep it descriptive — this is not a screening tool.
studies.wider_angle: A broader piece on the resurgence of vagal-tone measurement in psychology, from heart-rate-variability wearables to therapy apps, and how much of the popular "vagus nerve" discourse the evidence actually supports. Fits a consumer-health or skeptical-science outlet.
studies.caveats: Observational, self-reported trauma, stress and sleep; sex-specific moderation in a single sample; Chinese adolescent cohort, may not generalize.

studies.title: People who had tough childhoods react hardest to stress when they quit smoking
studies.ns_score_reason: a neat experimental manipulation of withdrawal with objective cardiovascular outcomes; modest N per group.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Smokers were randomized to smoke as usual (n=49) or abstain for 24 hours (n=69), alongside 45 non-smokers. All completed two identical sessions of speech preparation, speech delivery and mental arithmetic while blood pressure and heart rate were measured repeatedly. Exposure to at least one early-life adversity was associated with markedly larger systolic blood-pressure responses to stress — but only in the withdrawal group, not in ad libitum smokers or non-smokers.
studies.why_it_matters: It offers a concrete physiological reason why early adversity predicts relapse: the first day without nicotine may hit stress-reactive bodies harder, rather than simply testing willpower.
studies.pitch_angle: The surprise is the interaction — adversity did nothing to stress reactivity until nicotine was withdrawn, and then it did a lot. Open on day one of a quit attempt. Call Mustafa al'Absi at the University of Minnesota Medical School, Duluth, whose group has tracked stress biology and relapse for years. Avoid implying any clinical protocol change.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on why smoking-cessation success is stratified by childhood circumstances and social class, and what that means for cessation services that assume a level playing field — for a public-health or social-policy outlet.
studies.caveats: Moderate group sizes; randomization was to withdrawal condition, not to adversity, so the adversity comparison is observational; retrospective adversity report; short-term laboratory outcome, not relapse itself.

studies.title: Female footballers' anxiety and depression symptoms peak in the middle of the season
studies.ns_score_reason: rare four-wave longitudinal data in a group with almost none; self-report screeners, not diagnoses.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: 406 German female soccer players across six amateur and five elite clubs, aged from 12 to over 25, completed depression and anxiety screeners at four points across a season. Between 20% and 30% scored above threshold for anxiety and 15-25% for depression. Latent growth models showed symptoms were largely stable within individuals but followed significant linear and quadratic trends, peaking around mid-season.
studies.why_it_matters: It gives coaches and sport psychologists an actual calendar — a period when symptoms cluster — rather than a one-off prevalence figure, in a group whose profile has risen far faster than its support structures.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the timing: the mental-health dip isn't at the brutal pre-season or the title decider but in the unglamorous middle, when academic pressure, accumulated physical strain and performance expectations overlap. Open on a 16-year-old academy player in February. Call Leslie Carleton-Schweitzer at Heidelberg. Note that screeners measure symptoms, not disorders.
studies.wider_angle: A sports-desk feature on the support gap between men's and women's professional soccer — squad sizes, salaries, psychology staffing — set against the sport's commercial boom. Fits a sports or general-interest outlet.
studies.caveats: Self-reported screening instruments, not clinical diagnoses; German clubs only, may not generalize; no comparison group of non-athletes; attrition across four waves not specified in the abstract.

studies.title: Group therapy run inside a war zone proves workable for Ukrainian outpatients
studies.ns_score_reason: striking retention and effect sizes under extraordinary conditions, but single-arm with no control group.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: A culturally adapted modular "Empowerment" group therapy was delivered to 56 Ukrainian adult outpatients in five groups (three in person, two online) during the ongoing war. Retention was 96.4%, dropout 3.6%, protocol adherence 93%, and satisfaction high. Secondary outcomes showed large improvements in depressive symptoms (d=1.44), mental health-related quality of life (d=1.28), PTSD symptoms (d=1.18) and somatic symptom burden (d=1.16), with face-to-face groups generally doing better than online.
studies.why_it_matters: The prevailing assumption is that structured group psychotherapy is unworkable while bombardment continues; this pilot suggests it is deliverable and well accepted, and that in-person delivery may beat remote even when travel is dangerous.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is the 96% retention figure — people kept coming to group therapy through an active war, and the in-person groups outperformed the online ones despite the risk of getting there. Open on a Kyiv outpatient clinic session interrupted by an alert. Call Solveig Kemna at Charité and the Bogomolets National Medical University co-authors in Kyiv. Be clear the uncontrolled design means the effect sizes are not attributable to the therapy alone.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on how psychological intervention is being redesigned for populations still inside the traumatic event, rather than afterwards — challenging the "post" in post-traumatic. Fits a humanitarian, global-health or foreign-affairs outlet.
studies.caveats: Small N (56); single-arm with no control group, so improvement cannot be attributed to the intervention; short follow-up; self-reported outcomes.

studies.title: Supervisor support does more for remote workers the longer they stay remote
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuine 10-month panel with a time-varying effect, but modest N and self-reported throughout.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: 145 employees were surveyed at multiple points over 10 months of extended working from home. As the remote period lengthened, supervisor support became *increasingly* effective at blunting the effect of job demands and perceived stress on burnout — and reduced burnout in turn sustained work engagement.
studies.why_it_matters: Most remote-work research treats managerial support as a constant buffer; this suggests its value grows over time, which matters for organizations deciding whether check-ins are worth keeping once remote work stops being novel.
studies.pitch_angle: The counterintuitive bit is the direction of the trend — support mattered least at the start of home working and most months in, exactly when most managers let it lapse. Open on a manager quietly dropping the weekly one-to-one in month six. Call Shi-Woei Lin at National Taiwan University of Science and Technology. Keep it descriptive: this is a moderated panel model, not an experiment.
studies.wider_angle: A business-desk piece on what the return-to-office fight is really arguing about — presence versus support — using this and similar longitudinal data to ask whether mandates are solving a problem that better management would solve more cheaply.
studies.caveats: Small N (145); all self-reported; single national and occupational context, may not generalize; no randomization, so the moderation is correlational.

studies.title: Toddlers' sleep splits into two types — and bedtime struggles with parents mark the difference
studies.ns_score_reason: relatable and methodologically neat multidimensional profiling; entirely parent-reported.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Parents of 320 Canadian children aged 1-5 reported on sleep duration, timing, onset latency and quality, plus bedtime routines, parent-child sleep interactions, parental stress and the sleep environment. Latent profile analysis produced two groups — "Sleepy Koalas" (59%) and "Restless Racoons" (41%), the latter sleeping less, later, and worse on every dimension. Children from households earning over $100,000 were twice as likely to be Sleepy Koalas, and among preschoolers each one-unit increase in problematic parent-child sleep interaction cut the odds of good-sleeper membership by 21%.
studies.why_it_matters: It shifts attention from single metrics like "hours slept" to sleep as a package, and flags a socioeconomic gradient in children's sleep health that appears before school starts.
studies.pitch_angle: Sell the two animals: nearly half of young children fall into a pattern where short, late, slow-onset, poor-quality sleep all travel together, and the strongest modifiable correlate is the nightly negotiation at bedtime. Open on the 8pm standoff every parent knows. Call Valerie Carson at the University of Alberta. Do not turn a cross-sectional association into bedtime advice.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on sleep as an inequality marker across the life course — from toddler bedtimes to shift work — and why sleep is largely absent from child-health policy. Fits a social-policy or parenting-focused outlet.
studies.caveats: All measures parent-reported, including sleep; cross-sectional (cannot establish causation); online convenience sample of Canadian parents, may not generalize; parent-child interaction analyzed only in preschoolers.

studies.title: "Pregnancy brain" tracks mood, not pregnancy — and exercise softens the link
studies.ns_score_reason: a widely believed folk phenomenon gets a mood-based explanation; small sample limits confidence.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: 56 women from a longitudinal cohort were assessed at 28-30 weeks' gestation and six weeks postpartum for physical activity, anxiety and depressive symptoms, and everyday cognitive failures — the lapses of perception, memory and action that people mean by "baby brain." Higher prenatal mood symptoms predicted more cognitive failures both before and after birth. Physical activity showed no direct association with cognition, but meeting prenatal activity guidelines flattened the relationship between depressive symptoms and cognitive failures.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the forgetfulness women report in pregnancy is better predicted by mood than by pregnancy per se — a reframing with obvious consequences for how the complaint is dismissed or taken seriously.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead on the reframe: "pregnancy brain" may largely be anxiety and low mood brain, which is a very different clinical conversation. Open on a pregnant woman apologizing for losing her train of thought in a meeting. Call Danielle Symons Downs at Penn State. Flag the small sample explicitly and resist an exercise prescription.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on how routinely women's cognitive complaints across the reproductive lifespan — pregnancy, postpartum, menopause — get folk-explained by hormones while mood and sleep go unexamined. Fits a women's-health or general-interest magazine.
studies.caveats: Small N (56); self-reported cognition and activity; observational secondary analysis of a cohort; moderation findings were exploratory and partly inconsistent in direction; short follow-up (six weeks postpartum).

studies.title: Feeling that your life has gone off-course drains the good feelings, but doesn't add bad ones
studies.ns_score_reason: three studies including an experimental stress induction, and a useful set of nulls; the positive findings are thin.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Three studies tested whether "derailment" — the sense that your identity and life direction have been disrupted — makes stress hit harder. Study 1 (N=460 undergraduates, cross-sectional) failed to find the predicted interaction with perceived stress. Study 2 (N=224) used an online Trier Social Stress Test and found that acute stress moderated derailment's link to *positive* affect only. Study 3 (N=325) manipulated performance feedback and found no derailment-by-feedback interaction. Across all three, derailment consistently tracked diminished positive affect, not elevated negative affect.
studies.why_it_matters: It points to an asymmetry that keeps turning up in emotion research — the same conditions that blunt pleasure don't necessarily generate distress — and it reports its own failed predictions honestly.
studies.pitch_angle: The story is the asymmetry plus the nulls: feeling unmoored from who you were doesn't make you miserable, it makes you flat, and two of the three hypothesized interactions simply didn't appear. Open on someone six months after a career or relationship rupture who says nothing is wrong, just nothing is good. Call Anthony Burrow's group at Cornell, who built the derailment construct.
studies.wider_angle: A piece for a psychology or general-science outlet on anhedonia as the underrated core of modern distress — why "I feel nothing much" is harder to notice, diagnose and treat than "I feel terrible."
studies.caveats: Mostly student and online samples, may not generalize; primary hypotheses not supported in two of three studies; key positive finding is exploratory and nonlinear; self-reported affect throughout.

studies.title: Chronic stress is the single best lever against teenage self-harm — but the route differs by gender
studies.ns_score_reason: large sample and an interesting simulation approach, but the "interventions" are entirely in silico on cross-sectional data.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Researchers measured non-suicidal self-injury, chronic stress and emotion regulation in 2114 Chinese university students, built Ising network models, and then simulated knocking out individual nodes to see which would reduce self-injury most. Dysfunctional cognitive reappraisal drove self-injury behaviors in women; emotional suppression drove self-injury functions in men. Reducing chronic stress produced the largest simulated reduction in both groups.
studies.why_it_matters: Network simulation is being pitched as a way to prioritize intervention targets without running dozens of trials; this is a readable test case, though the result remains a hypothesis to be tested in real trials.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead on the method as much as the finding — researchers are now running "virtual interventions" on psychological networks to decide what to test in people, and here the winner was not emotion-regulation training but simply lowering chronic stress. Open on the simulation itself. Call Xue Yang at Southern Medical University. Be firm that no one has yet done this intervention in a real teenager.
studies.wider_angle: A methods feature for a specialist psychology or data-science outlet on the rise and contested validity of network psychometrics — whether symptom networks are causal maps or elaborate correlation pictures.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional data (cannot establish causation); "interventions" are simulated, not performed; Chinese university sample, may not generalize; self-reported self-injury.

studies.title: Gender outranks every psychological factor in predicting teenage gaming disorder
studies.ns_score_reason: big sample and thorough model evaluation, but cross-sectional and the top predictor is unmodifiable.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Four machine-learning algorithms were trained on data from 6573 adolescents to classify internet gaming disorder, with a random forest performing best. SHAP analysis ranked predictors: gender first, then depressive symptoms, insomnia, social anxiety, emotional abuse, health adaptation problems, anxiety, academic stress and punishment experiences. Network analysis put anxiety, academic stress and health adaptation at the center of the web.
studies.why_it_matters: It positions problem gaming less as a gaming problem and more as a stress-and-distress problem, with academic pressure sitting at the structural center — though nothing here establishes direction of effect.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is what the model *didn't* rank highly: nothing about games themselves. After gender, the list is depression, insomnia, social anxiety and abuse — which reads like a distress profile, not a hobby. Open on a parent confiscating a console. Call Yanmei Shen at the Second Xiangya Hospital of Central South University. Do not let the machine-learning framing imply prediction of individual cases.
studies.wider_angle: A reported feature on the contested diagnosis itself — internet gaming disorder's uneasy status in DSM and ICD, and the researchers who argue it pathologizes a coping strategy rather than a disease. Fits a technology or general-interest outlet.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional (cannot establish causation); self-reported measures throughout; single-country adolescent sample, may not generalize; feature importance rankings are model-dependent.

studies.title: People start therapy when their symptoms spike — not when their lives get harder
studies.ns_score_reason: an unusually long within-person design with a clean null on stressors; the main result confirms expectations.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: 1417 participants completed up to seven annual assessments of depressive symptoms, family and friend support, self-reported stressors, and treatment use. Multilevel models separating within-person from between-person variation showed that when an individual's depressive symptoms rose above their own usual level, they were more likely to be in treatment that year and the next. Fluctuations in social support and in stressful life events were only inconsistently related to treatment use once symptoms were accounted for.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests help-seeking is triggered by internal symptom change rather than by external circumstance — so people going through objectively hard periods without symptom escalation may go unserved.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the null: losing your social support or being hit by life events did not reliably send people into treatment; only feeling worse than your own baseline did. Open on someone whose annus horribilis never produced a therapy appointment. Call Thomas Olino at Temple University, and ask what this implies for services organized around life-event triggers such as bereavement or job loss.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on the mismatch between how mental health services are marketed — around crises and events — and how people actually decide to seek help, for a health-services or social-policy outlet.
studies.caveats: Observational (cannot establish causation); self-reported symptoms, stressors and treatment use; annual assessments may miss short-lived episodes; the headline within-person symptom result is confirmatory rather than novel.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- PTSD keeps behaving like a whole-body condition. The previous digest's population epidemiology, "Men recover from PTSD in about a decade — for women it takes twice as long" (PMID 42303590), flagged PTSD's links to asthma and diabetes as a wider angle; this run makes that the main event, with "Anxiety disorders and PTSD are linked to a higher risk of stroke" (PMID 42767516) and "Treating PTSD reduces physical pain — even when no one treats the pain" (PMID 42766718).
- The measurement-mode split continues. Last run it was "Brain stimulation for PTSD works on questionnaires but not on clinician interviews" (PMID 42680058) and the publication-bias reversal in bullying therapy (PMID 42658011); this run the same fault line runs through "Stress hormones show up in how other people rate your working relationships" (PMID 42667999) and "A close bond with parents fails to protect stressed teenagers' response to reward" (PMID 42773853), where self-report, behavior and EEG give three different answers about one construct.
- Adversity effects keep turning out to be conditional rather than main effects. Following "When childhood abuse happens may matter more than how much of it there was" (PMID 42683544), this run adds "People who had tough childhoods react hardest to stress when they quit smoking" (PMID 42771860), where early adversity did nothing to cardiovascular reactivity until nicotine was withdrawn, and "Childhood trauma shows up in teenagers' sleep years later" (PMID 42785565), where perceived stress, not the trauma itself, is the operative step.
- Honest reversals of favored hypotheses are becoming the batch's signature. Last run: chronic stress blunting rather than amplifying daily reactivity (PMID 42595230) and the cognitive-reserve/loneliness paradox (PMID 42687444). This run: the failed parental buffering result (PMID 42773853) and the three-study derailment package with two unsupported predictions (PMID 42765820).

**Advances**
- Suicide research moves one step down the pathway. The previous digest predicted ideation — loneliness as an independent prospective risk factor (PMID 42642073) and the partly non-replicating IMV moderation (PMID 42683538). "Post-traumatic stress symptoms predict who moves from suicidal thoughts to an attempt" (PMID 42705422) tackles the harder ideation-to-attempt transition in a sample already at risk, and finds OCD symptoms running protectively — a capability-style result the IMV work did not test.
- War as a stress exposure moves from description to intervention. Last run offered "Growing up in a war zone changes which brain circuits track a child's attachment style" (PMID 42607893) and sociopolitical climate as trauma (PMID 42658624); this run delivers treatment inside the exposure with "Group therapy run inside a war zone proves workable for Ukrainian outpatients" (PMID 42731584).
- The sport thread gains a time axis. "Children whose parents and coaches both push winning report the most stress" (PMID 42419608) was a cross-sectional profile; "Female footballers' anxiety and depression symptoms peak in the middle of the season" (PMID 42759733) gives four waves and a seasonal shape.

**Counterpoints**
- Cortisol's status shifts again. "Mindfulness courses genuinely lower levels of the stress hormone cortisol" (PMID 42691284) treated cortisol as the hard outcome that vindicates soft self-reports; "Stress hormones show up in how other people rate your working relationships" (PMID 42667999) finds cortisol tracking *observer*-rated behavior while self-reports of the same relationships stay flat. Together they suggest cortisol is informative about things people do not notice about themselves — useful nuance for anyone writing cortisol as a straightforward stress readout.

**New themes**
- A perinatal cluster with no precedent in the previous run: "About half of postpartum depression cases don't lift within the first year" (PMID 42749161) and "'Pregnancy brain' tracks mood, not pregnancy" (PMID 42764724).
- Simulation and machine-learning methods used to rank intervention targets: "Chronic stress is the single best lever against teenage self-harm" (PMID 42788378) and "Gender outranks every psychological factor in predicting teenage gaming disorder" (PMID 42732833). The previous digest's network work (PMID 42695429) was descriptive; these papers try to make networks prescriptive.
- Immune-to-brain-clearance mechanism enters the topic with "Inflammation in the body changes what brain-clearance markers mean in depressed teenage girls" (PMID 42777933).
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** A striking number of studies here find that stress registers where the stressed person cannot see it. Probation officers' daily cortisol predicted how observers rated their fairness and trustworthiness but had no relationship to the officers' own ratings of the same encounters (PMID 42667999); people entered therapy when their depressive symptoms rose above their personal baseline, while losing social support or being hit by life events did not reliably send them in (PMID 42732668); feeling your life has gone off-course drained positive affect without producing the distress everyone predicts (PMID 42765820); and the forgetfulness women call "pregnancy brain" tracked mood symptoms rather than pregnancy itself (PMID 42764724). "A close bond with parents fails to protect stressed teenagers' response to reward" (PMID 42773853) makes the same point about measurement: self-report, behavior and the brain's reward response to money disagreed within the same adolescents.

**Why pitch this now:** Mental health services, workplace wellness programs and app-based screening all run on the assumption that people can report their own stress accurately and will seek help when life gets objectively hard — and this batch, arriving together, suggests both assumptions fail in specific, predictable ways.

**Angle:** A reported feature on the limits of stress introspection — what other people, hormones and reaction-time tasks know about your stress before you do, and what that means for services built around self-referral and self-report. For general readers with an interest in psychology, plus clinicians and managers who design screening around questionnaires.

**Potential headlines:**
- Stressed people rate their own relationships the same on good days and bad ones
- A terrible year won't send you to therapy — a bad month relative to your own baseline will
- The stress you can't feel is the one no service will catch

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features (Mind)** — the section already runs construct-under-revision pieces, and the cortisol-versus-observer-ratings study gives a vivid, concrete opening scene.
- **The Atlantic** — strong fit for the help-seeking mismatch: why objectively hard lives don't produce therapy appointments, and who that leaves unserved.
- **BBC Future** — has a steady line in "what your body knows before you do" psychology, and can carry the physiological detail without losing general readers.
- **Aeon** — the deeper strand here is the failure of introspection as a data source about one's own state, which suits Aeon's psychology-and-mind essays.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Stress — September 2026
**Checked:** 2026-09-26 | **Studies reviewed:** 18
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

# Fact-Check Report — New Scientist Mind digest, run date 2026-09-26

---

### Study 1: Anxiety disorders and PTSD are linked to a higher risk of stroke, in a pooled analysis of 11 million people
**PMID:** 42767516 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Sample (23 cohorts, 11,181,338 participants), HRs (1.29 anxiety = 29%; 1.50 PTSD = 50%), persistence after adjustment for cardiovascular risk factors and depression, and the OCD single-study caveat all check out.

**Issue A. Unsupported comparison with depression** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "The surprise is that PTSD outperformed depression — the usual psychiatric suspect in cardiovascular risk"
- **Abstract says:** "Associations persisted after adjustment for cardiovascular risk factors and depression." No pooled effect estimate for depression is reported, and no head-to-head comparison is described.
- **Problem:** The meta-analysis adjusted *for* depression; it did not estimate depression's own stroke hazard, so it cannot show PTSD "outperforming" it. A writer taking this hook to an editor would be pitching a result the paper does not contain.
- **Suggested fix:** "The surprise is that the PTSD association survived adjustment for depression — the usual psychiatric suspect in cardiovascular risk — suggesting it is not simply depression in disguise."

**Issue B. Hemorrhagic stroke framed as a null** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the association held specifically for ischemic (not hemorrhagic) stroke"
- **Abstract says:** "Associations were observed for ischaemic stroke (HR 1.34, 95% CI 1.13-1.58), whereas haemorrhagic stroke did not reach statistical significance (HR 1.24, 95% CI 0.95-1.62)."
- **Problem:** The hemorrhagic point estimate is similar in size; it simply failed to reach significance, likely a power issue. "Not hemorrhagic" implies a demonstrated absence of effect.
- **Suggested fix:** "the association was statistically significant for ischemic stroke, while the hemorrhagic estimate was similar in size but did not reach significance"

**Issue C. Named confounders not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the link survived adjustment for blood pressure, smoking and the rest"
- **Abstract says:** "adjustment for cardiovascular risk factors and depression" (unspecified).
- **Problem:** Which specific risk factors were adjusted for is unverifiable from abstract only; naming blood pressure and smoking is an assumption.
- **Suggested fix:** "the link survived adjustment for conventional cardiovascular risk factors (check the paper for the specific covariate list)"

*NS fit 7/10:* defensible — 11 million participants pooled from longitudinal cohorts, with the observational limit explicitly priced in.

---

### Study 2: Stress hormones show up in how other people rate your working relationships — not in how you rate them yourself
**PMID:** 42667999 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

All counts (46 officers, four waves, 2126 sessions, 732 supervisees, 432 self-rated), both directional effects (log AUCg → Caring/Fairness; flatter slope → Trust), and the self-report null are reproduced correctly.

**Issue A. Causal verb in "Why it matters"** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "It suggests physiological stress degrades the skilled, effortful part of professional interaction"
- **Abstract says:** "HPA dysregulation covaries with what independent observers see in professional relational behavior but not with what the professional perceives."
- **Problem:** "Degrades" asserts causation from a within-person correlational design. The pitch angle correctly says "this is covariation, not proof that cortisol causes worse behavior" — but the body text contradicts that caution, and the body is what an editor reads first.
- **Suggested fix:** "It suggests physiological stress covaries with the skilled, effortful part of professional interaction — and does so invisibly to the person doing it"

**Issue B. NS fit score** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "NS fit: 7/10"
- **Problem:** The unit of analysis for the cortisol predictor is 46 professionals in a single occupational setting, with no experimental control; the 2126 sessions inflate the apparent sample. The observer-rated (rather than self-reported) outcome is a genuine strength, which keeps this from being a serious overscore.
- **Suggested fix:** Score 6/10.

---

### Study 3: A close bond with parents fails to protect stressed teenagers' response to reward
**PMID:** 42773853 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=165, ages 9-16, 78.18% White, the three measurement modalities, and the contrary-to-prediction blunted monetary RewP and reduced behavioral reward sensitivity are all accurate. Caveats correctly note the non-significant interactions.

**Issue A. "Overturns prior research" overstates a single contrary-to-hypothesis result** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** Overturns prior research" / headline "A close bond with parents fails to protect stressed teenagers' response to reward"
- **Abstract says:** "The results suggest that high-quality PCR may *not uniformly* buffer against the effects of peer stress exposure and highlight differential effects for different PVS measures."
- **Problem:** The finding was contrary to the authors' own predictions on two of several outcome measures, with no significant interaction elsewhere. That is a qualification of the buffering hypothesis, not an overturning of it, and the headline's flat "fails to protect" generalizes beyond the two measures that moved.
- **Suggested fix:** Novelty: "Contrary to prediction." Headline: "A close bond with parents doesn't uniformly protect stressed teenagers' response to reward."

---

### Study 4: Treating PTSD reduces physical pain — even when no one treats the pain
**PMID:** 42766718 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=196, the three randomized arms, 52 weeks, the n=70 / n=93 subgroups, and the PE+PLB advantage on pain interference are all correct. Industry and foundation relationships are properly flagged in Caveats.

**Issue A. Causal headline from a secondary analysis with no pain-only or no-treatment control** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Treating PTSD reduces physical pain — even when no one treats the pain"
- **Abstract says:** "While it is uncertain reduced pain was due to the treatments themselves, lower scores for all treatments suggest that PTSD-focused treatments *may* reduce pain even without a specific pain focus."
- **Problem:** The authors explicitly decline to attribute the pain reduction to treatment, because all arms improved and there is no control for the passage of time. The headline states as established what the paper states as uncertain. The Caveats note this, but the headline is the pitch.
- **Suggested fix:** "Pain fell during PTSD treatment — even though no one was treating the pain"

---

### Study 5: Post-traumatic stress symptoms predict who moves from suicidal thoughts to an attempt
**PMID:** 42705422 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N=923, mean age 36.2, 65.2% women, 6-monthly follow-up over 18 months, 86% retention, 11.5% (106) attempts, PTSD HR 1.264, smaller depressive HR, and the negative OCD association (HR 0.960) all match. Framing is appropriately hedged, the attenuation by lifetime attempt history is carried into Caveats, and the suicide-reporting guidance is sound.

---

### Study 6: About half of postpartum depression cases don't lift within the first year
**PMID:** 42749161 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=191, 12-month repeated measures, 4.7% and 25.6% figures, and the persistent-case risk correlates are all accurate.

**Issue A. Baby blues + PMS signature attributed to the wrong trajectory group** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Note the hormonal-sensitivity signature — baby blues plus PMS — as an observational pattern, not a test."
- **Abstract says:** "In contrast, the *recovering* cases reported frequent baby blues and PMS, which can be understood as proxy indicators of a heightened hormonal sensitivity."
- **Problem:** The digest body lists PMS among the *persistent* case markers (correct) and then invokes the baby-blues-plus-PMS signature without saying it characterized the *recovering* group. A writer could easily pitch it as a persistence marker, reversing the prognostic direction.
- **Suggested fix:** "Note the hormonal-sensitivity signature — frequent baby blues plus PMS — which marked the *recovering* cases, not the persistent ones; an observational pattern, not a test."

**Issue B. "Overturns prior research" is too strong** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** Overturns prior research"
- **Abstract says:** "its long-term progression and the underlying mechanisms of its different trajectories remain poorly understood."
- **Problem:** The paper fills a gap in trajectory data rather than contradicting established findings; the 4-6 week framing is described as incomplete, not wrong.
- **Suggested fix:** Novelty: "Extends prior research / new trajectory data."

---

### Study 7: Inflammation in the body changes what brain-clearance markers mean in depressed teenage girls
**PMID:** 42777933 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=461 MDD and 253 controls, the multimodal glymphatic markers, the higher SII, and the sex-specific SII × choroid plexus volume moderation are all faithfully reported, as is the "mechanistic lead, not clinical" framing.

**Issue A. Direction of the perivascular diffusion finding is left vague** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Depressed adolescents showed altered perivascular diffusion, higher free water and a higher systemic immune-inflammation index."
- **Abstract says:** "adolescents with MDD exhibited a significantly *elevated* diffusion tensor imaging along the perivascular space index, increased free water fraction, and higher systemic immune-inflammation index (SII) levels."
- **Problem:** "Altered" obscures the direction. An elevated DTI-ALPS index is conventionally read as *greater* perivascular diffusivity, which sits awkwardly with the "glymphatic dysfunction" framing a writer would reach for; the vagueness invites a wrong-direction pitch.
- **Suggested fix:** "Depressed adolescents showed an elevated perivascular diffusion (DTI-ALPS) index, higher free water and a higher systemic immune-inflammation index."

---

### Study 8: Childhood trauma shows up in teenagers' sleep years later — and perceived stress is the route
**PMID:** 42785565 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=284, the baseline/1.5-year measurement structure, the mediation by perceived stress after controlling for baseline sleep, and the male-only RSA-suppression moderation (weaker stress–sleep link at higher suppression) are all correct.

**Issue A. Unverifiable task detail** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "how hard a teenager's vagus nerve pulls back during a three-minute speech task"
- **Abstract says:** "a speech task during which their data of vagal regulation indexed by respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA) suppression was obtained at baseline." No duration given.
- **Problem:** The three-minute figure is Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** Drop the duration or confirm from full text: "how hard a teenager's vagus nerve pulls back during a stressful speech task".

**Issue B. "Years later" and "is the route"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Childhood trauma shows up in teenagers' sleep years later — and perceived stress is the route"
- **Abstract says:** Follow-up was "1.5 years later"; perceived stress "mediated this association" in an observational design.
- **Problem:** "Years later" inflates an 18-month gap (the body text gets it right), and "is the route" states a causal pathway that statistical mediation on observational data cannot establish.
- **Suggested fix:** "Childhood trauma shows up in teenagers' sleep 18 months later — and perceived stress tracks the link"

---

### Study 9: People who had tough childhoods react hardest to stress when they quit smoking
**PMID:** 42771860 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Group sizes (49 ad libitum, 69 withdrawal, 45 non-smokers), randomization to smoking condition, the two identical sessions with speech preparation/delivery and mental arithmetic, and the significant group × ELA interaction for SBP are all accurate. Caveats correctly note that the adversity comparison is observational.

**Issue A. Specificity claim goes beyond the reported contrast** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "but only in the withdrawal group, not in ad libitum smokers or non-smokers" / "adversity did nothing to stress reactivity until nicotine was withdrawn, and then it did a lot"
- **Abstract says:** "The effect of having ≥1 ELA event on SBP changes in the withdrawal group was significantly greater than that in non-smokers (fixed effect = 3.89; 95% CI = 1.41 to 6.36; P=0.002)."
- **Problem:** Only the withdrawal-versus-non-smoker contrast is reported. Whether ad libitum smokers differed is not stated, and "did nothing" asserts a null that the abstract never reports. "Did a lot" also overstates a ~3.9 mmHg fixed effect.
- **Suggested fix:** "Exposure to at least one early-life adversity was associated with larger systolic blood-pressure responses to stress in the withdrawal group than in non-smokers (about 3.9 mmHg). Check the full text before claiming ad libitum smokers showed no effect."

**Issue B. "Markedly larger"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "markedly larger systolic blood-pressure responses to stress"
- **Abstract says:** "fixed effect = 3.89; 95% CI = 1.41 to 6.36"
- **Problem:** A ~4 mmHg difference in stress reactivity is statistically clear but modest; "markedly" oversells it.
- **Suggested fix:** "measurably larger systolic blood-pressure responses to stress (about 4 mmHg)"

*Note:* al'Absi's University of Minnesota Duluth affiliation is Unverifiable from abstract only (no affiliations listed for this record).

---

### Study 10: Female footballers' anxiety and depression symptoms peak in the middle of the season
**PMID:** 42759733 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=406, six amateur and five elite German clubs, the age bands, four time points, the 20-30% / 15-25% threshold figures, and the latent growth finding of stability plus significant linear and quadratic trends peaking mid-season are all correct. The "screeners, not diagnoses" caution is well placed.

**Issue A. Authors' speculation presented as finding** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "in the unglamorous middle, when academic pressure, accumulated physical strain and performance expectations overlap"
- **Abstract says:** "players *might* experience increased performance pressure, academic stress, or accumulated physical strain."
- **Problem:** The abstract offers these as untested explanations for the mid-season peak; the digest presents them as the established mechanism.
- **Suggested fix:** "in the unglamorous middle — a period the authors speculate may combine academic pressure, accumulated physical strain and performance expectations, though the study did not test that"

---

### Study 11: Group therapy run inside a war zone proves workable for Ukrainian outpatients
**PMID:** 42731584 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=56, five groups (3 face-to-face, 2 online), retention 96.4%, dropout 3.6%, adherence 93%, and the effect sizes (PHQ-9 d=1.44; SF-36 Mental Health d=1.28; PCL-5 d=1.18; SSS-8 d=1.16) all match. The uncontrolled-design caution is stated in both the pitch and the Caveats.

**Issue A. "Proves" in the headline** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Group therapy run inside a war zone proves workable for Ukrainian outpatients"
- **Abstract says:** "This pilot shows the implementation of Empowerment group therapy is feasible in Ukrainian outpatients during an ongoing war," with progression to an RCT recommended.
- **Problem:** "Proves" is stronger than a 56-person single-arm feasibility pilot supports, even where progression criteria were met.
- **Suggested fix:** "Group therapy run inside a war zone looks deliverable for Ukrainian outpatients, a pilot finds"

**Issue B. Face-to-face versus online comparison** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the in-person groups outperformed the online ones despite the risk of getting there"
- **Abstract says:** "Improvements were generally larger in face-to-face groups," and the conclusion calls for future work "to clarify optimal delivery conditions for in-person versus online formats."
- **Problem:** Participants were not randomized to format and no statistical comparison is reported; "outperformed" reads as a tested difference. The "Why it matters" hedges with "may beat," but the pitch angle does not.
- **Suggested fix:** "improvements were generally larger in the in-person groups, though format was not randomized and the difference wasn't formally tested"

---

### Study 12: Supervisor support does more for remote workers the longer they stay remote
**PMID:** 42777487 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N=145, multiple time points over 10 months, the time-varying moderation (supervisor support becoming increasingly effective at alleviating job demands and perceived stress on burnout), and the burnout → sustained engagement chain all match the abstract. Framing stays correlational and the Caveats note the absence of randomization.

*Note:* the Caveat "single national and occupational context" is Unverifiable from abstract only — no sample nationality or sector is stated — but as a hedge it does no harm.

---

### Study 13: Toddlers' sleep splits into two types — and bedtime struggles with parents mark the difference
**PMID:** 42764403 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=320 Canadian children aged 1-5, parent-reported online questionnaire, the two latent profiles (59% / 41%) and their dimensional contrasts, the income OR of 2.05, and the 21% lower odds per unit of problematic parent-child sleep interaction in preschoolers are all accurate.

**Issue A. "Toddlers" mislabels the age range** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Toddlers' sleep splits into two types"
- **Abstract says:** "320 children aged 1-5 years," with the parent-child sleep interaction analysis restricted to "preschoolers aged 3-5 years only."
- **Problem:** The headline's "toddlers" covers only part of a 1-5 range, and the interaction finding it pairs with applies to the preschool subgroup only. The Caveats flag the second half, but the headline still misstates the population.
- **Suggested fix:** "Young children's sleep splits into two types — and bedtime struggles with parents mark the difference in preschoolers"

**Issue B. Causal verb for a cross-sectional association** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "each one-unit increase in problematic parent-child sleep interaction cut the odds of good-sleeper membership by 21%"
- **Abstract says:** "each one-unit increase in problematic interactions was *associated with* 21% lower likelihood of Sleepy Koalas membership."
- **Problem:** "Cut" implies the interaction produced the change; the design cannot separate cause from consequence (poor sleepers may generate more bedtime conflict).
- **Suggested fix:** "each one-unit increase in problematic parent-child sleep interaction was associated with 21% lower odds of good-sleeper membership"

**Issue C. Unsupported ranking of correlates** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the strongest modifiable correlate is the nightly negotiation at bedtime"
- **Abstract says:** Reports the income and parent-child interaction associations but does not rank correlates by strength or label any as modifiable.
- **Problem:** "Strongest modifiable correlate" is Unverifiable from abstract only and reads as a hierarchy the paper does not present.
- **Suggested fix:** "one of the few correlates a parent could plausibly change is the nightly negotiation at bedtime"

---

### Study 14: "Pregnancy brain" tracks mood, not pregnancy — and exercise softens the link
**PMID:** 42764724 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=56, the 28-30 week and 6-week postpartum timepoints, the mood–cognitive failures association, and the absence of a direct PA–cognition association are all correct. Caveats commendably flag that the moderation findings were exploratory and inconsistent in direction.

**Issue A. "Not pregnancy" is untestable in this design** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "'Pregnancy brain' tracks mood, not pregnancy" / "the forgetfulness women report in pregnancy is better predicted by mood than by pregnancy per se"
- **Abstract says:** "Higher prenatal mood symptoms were associated with greater prenatal and postpartum cognitive failures." All 56 participants were pregnant; there is no non-pregnant comparison group.
- **Problem:** With no non-pregnant control, the study cannot compare mood against pregnancy as competing explanations. It shows that within pregnant women, mood symptoms track cognitive failures — a much narrower claim than the headline.
- **Suggested fix:** "'Pregnancy brain' tracks mood symptoms — and exercise may soften the link"

**Issue B. Headline states an exploratory, inconsistent moderation as established** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "and exercise softens the link"
- **Abstract says:** "*exploratory analyses* examined whether PA modified relationships"; the moderation ran in the expected direction for depressive symptoms in the meet-PA group, but for anxiety symptoms the lower rate was in the *not* meeting postpartum PA guidelines group.
- **Problem:** Half the moderation evidence runs the opposite way. The Caveats say so; the headline does not.
- **Suggested fix:** "— and meeting activity guidelines may soften part of it (exploratory)"

---

### Study 15: Feeling that your life has gone off-course drains the good feelings, but doesn't add bad ones
**PMID:** 42765820 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

The three-study structure, sample sizes (460 / 224 / 325), the non-significant hypothesized interactions in Studies 1 and 3, the positive-affect-only moderation in Study 2, and the overall conclusion are all reported accurately — including the nulls, which is to the digest's credit.

**Issue A. Causal language for a measured individual difference** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Feeling that your life has gone off-course drains the good feelings, but doesn't add bad ones" / "feeling unmoored from who you were doesn't make you miserable, it makes you flat"
- **Abstract says:** "Derailment was most consistently *related to* diminished positive affect."
- **Problem:** Derailment was measured, never manipulated — only stress and feedback valence were experimentally varied. "Drains" and "makes you flat" assert a causal effect of derailment on affect that none of the three designs can support. This is not flagged in Caveats.
- **Suggested fix:** Headline: "Feeling that your life has gone off-course goes with fewer good feelings — not more bad ones." Pitch: "feeling unmoored from who you were isn't linked to more misery, but to less pleasure."

*NS fit 4/10:* defensible and appropriately modest given the nulls.

---

### Study 16: Chronic stress is the single best lever against teenage self-harm — but the route differs by gender
**PMID:** 42788378 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=2114, the Ising network and in silico intervention method, the gendered pathways (dysfunctional cognitive reappraisal → NSSI behaviors in females; emotional suppression → NSSI functions in males), and chronic stress as the top simulated target all match the abstract. The pitch and Caveats are admirably firm that nothing was actually intervened upon.

**Issue A. Headline states a simulated result as a demonstrated intervention effect** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Chronic stress is the single best lever against teenage self-harm"
- **Abstract says:** "chronic stress emerged as the most effective universal intervention target, producing the greatest NSSI reduction across genders" — in *in silico* interventions run on cross-sectional network models.
- **Problem:** "Is the single best lever" reads as an established treatment finding. Nothing was reduced in anyone; a node was knocked out in a model built from one-time questionnaire data. The body and Caveats hedge, but the headline is the pitch, and it claims an intervention result.
- **Suggested fix:** "Simulations point to chronic stress as the top target for teenage self-harm — but the route differs by gender"

**Issue B. "Teenage" / "teenager" for a university-student sample** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "teenage self-harm"; "no one has yet done this intervention in a real teenager"
- **Abstract says:** "2114 Chinese university students" (the paper's own title says "adolescent").
- **Problem:** The sample is university students, most of whom will be over 19. The Caveats get this right; the headline and pitch do not.
- **Suggested fix:** "young people's self-harm" / "in a real student".

---

### Study 17: Gender outranks every psychological factor in predicting teenage gaming disorder
**PMID:** 42732833 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=6573, four algorithms with random forest selected, the SHAP ranking order, and the network centrality of anxiety, academic stress and health adaptation are all reproduced correctly. The caution against reading individual-level prediction into the ML framing is well judged.

**Issue A. The pitch hook rests on an unverifiable absence** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "The hook is what the model *didn't* rank highly: nothing about games themselves."
- **Abstract says:** The candidate features are described as "demographic and psychosocial factors" — early adversity, negative life events, psychological symptoms, regulatory emotional self-efficacy. No gaming-behavior variables (playtime, genre, spend) are mentioned as inputs.
- **Problem:** If gaming-behavior variables were never entered into the model, their absence from the SHAP ranking is a design choice, not a finding — and the pitch's entire hook collapses. Unverifiable from abstract only; must be checked in the full text before this angle is pitched.
- **Suggested fix:** "The hook is the shape of the ranking: after gender, it is depression, insomnia, social anxiety and emotional abuse — a distress profile. (Check whether gaming-behaviour variables were candidate features at all before framing this as an absence.)"

---

### Study 18: People start therapy when their symptoms spike — not when their lives get harder
**PMID:** 42732668 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=1417, up to seven annual assessments, the within/between-person disaggregation, and the concurrent-plus-next-year association of within-person symptom increases with treatment use are all accurate. The digest is honest that the main result is confirmatory.

**Issue A. "Clean null" overstates an inconsistent result** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "an unusually long within-person design with a clean null on stressors"
- **Abstract says:** "Fluctuations in family and friend support and self-reported stressors were *inconsistently* associated with treatment use controlling for depressive symptoms."
- **Problem:** "Inconsistently associated" means some associations appeared and some did not — not a clean null. The pitch angle's "did not reliably send people into treatment" is fine; the NS fit line is not.
- **Suggested fix:** "an unusually long within-person design in which stressors and support related only inconsistently to treatment use"

**Issue B. "Start therapy" versus treatment use** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "People start therapy when their symptoms spike"
- **Abstract says:** "individuals are more likely to *use* treatment when they are experiencing higher levels of symptoms than they usually experience."
- **Problem:** The outcome is annual treatment use, which mixes initiation with continuation; the study does not isolate the moment of entry into care.
- **Suggested fix:** "People are in therapy when their symptoms spike — not when their lives get harder"

**Cross-cutting note for the desk:** the recurring failure mode in this digest is not bad arithmetic — the numbers are almost uniformly right — but headlines that assert causation or intervention effects (Studies 4, 14, 15, 16) while the body text and Caveats correctly hedge. Editors read headlines first. Where the Caveats already say "cannot establish causation," the headline should not say "reduces," "drains," "is the best lever," or "tracks mood, not pregnancy."
